code.title: Each type gets its own instantiation

followUps: Implicit instantiation happens on its own when you use a template; explicit instantiation is you asking for it by name. Writing maxOf(1, 2) makes the compiler generate maxOf<int> implicitly, but only if the definition is visible there. Writing template int maxOf<int>(int, int); forces generation of that one specialization in this file even if nobody calls it. You use the explicit form to keep a template body in a .cpp file and still export a few known types, or to control which object file holds the code.

It tells the compiler: do not instantiate this template here, it exists in another file, so just emit a call. Example: a header says extern template class Matrix<double>; and one .cpp says template class Matrix<double>;. The 50 files including the header skip compiling Matrix<double> 50 times, so builds get faster and object files smaller. It is only an optimization; the program behaves the same without it.

Each file that needs the instantiation produces its own copy, but they are marked as weak or COMDAT symbols, so the linker keeps one and discards the rest. This is why templates in headers do not cause duplicate-symbol errors even though 10 object files all contain foo<int>. The linker can pick any copy because the language promises they are identical. Cost: the compiler still did the work 10 times, which is what extern template avoids.

code.title: Explicit instantiation for a closed set of types

followUps: No, because the ODR explicitly allows templates (and inline functions) to be defined in several translation units as long as every definition is token-for-token the same and means the same thing. That is why a header-defined template included in 20 .cpp files links fine. Violations happen when the definitions differ, for example when a macro changes the body in one file only. The compiler usually cannot catch that, and you get silent undefined behavior, so keep the header identical everywhere.

Modules compile the template once into a binary interface, so importers no longer re-parse thousands of header lines. A project with 200 files each including a 20,000-line template header parses that text 200 times; with a module it is parsed once. Instantiation still happens per use, so heavy instantiation is not removed. Gains are real but vary by compiler and build system: expect parsing time to drop sharply, while instantiation-bound code improves little.

code.title: Deduction for T, T& and T&&

followUps: A reference collapse rule says that a reference to a reference becomes a single reference, and the result is an lvalue reference if either one is. The rules are: T& &, T& && and T&& & all become T&; only T&& && stays T&&. You cannot write a reference to a reference yourself, but templates and aliases can produce one. This is why for an lvalue int x, a parameter T&& with T = int& becomes int&, which is the trick behind forwarding references.

Because auto x = e; is deduced exactly like template<class T> void f(T) called with e: top-level const and references are dropped, arrays decay. So auto a = 5 gives int, const auto& b = c keeps const. The one difference is braces: auto x = {1, 2} deduces std::initializer_list<int>, while a template parameter T cannot deduce from {1, 2} at all and fails.

Give the parameter the type std::initializer_list<T> and T is deduced from the elements: template<class T> void f(std::initializer_list<T> l) called as f({1, 2, 3}) gives T = int. All elements must deduce to the same type, so f({1, 2.5}) fails. A plain T parameter cannot do this, and auto x = {1, 2, 3} works only because auto has a special rule.

code.title: Overload ranking: templates vs normal functions

followUps: Because the compiler never even considers an explicit specialization when choosing which function to call; it only picks among the primary templates and overloads, and then uses a specialization of the winner if one exists. Here g(&x) with int* prefers g(T*) (T = int), which is more specialized than g(T). Your g<int*> specialization belongs to the first template g(T), which lost, so it is never used. Fix: write an ordinary overload void g(int*).

Writing f<>(x) means: only consider templates named f, and deduce all arguments from x. A non-template f(int) is excluded from the candidate set. Example with f(int) and template<class T> f(T): f(5) calls the non-template, but f<>(5) calls the template with T = int. It is handy to force the generic path or to name a specific template from a friend declaration.

code.title: Full and partial specialization

followUps: Only when the standard says so: you may fully specialize a standard library template, such as std::hash<MyKey> or std::formatter<MyType>, when it depends on a user-defined type and meets the library's requirements. Adding anything else to namespace std (new functions, overloads, partial specializations of function templates, specializing type traits like std::is_integral) is undefined behavior. To customize ordinary functions, put overloads in your own namespace so argument-dependent lookup finds them.

Because vector<bool> is specialized to pack 8 bools per byte, so it is not a container of bool anymore. operator[] returns a proxy object instead of bool&, so auto& b = v[0]; fails, &v[0] does not give a bool*, and generic code written for vector<T> breaks. Concurrent writes to two different elements can race on the same byte. Use vector<char> or std::bitset / dynamic_bitset equivalents.

code.title: Variadic templates and fold expressions

followUps: Only an empty pack's unary fold over &&, || or , is allowed; it gives true, false and void() respectively. Folds over +, * and the rest are errors for an empty pack, so use a binary fold with an init: (args + ... + 0) gives 0 for no arguments. Example: sum() with (args + ...) does not compile, while (args + ... + 0) returns 0.

No. The order in which the expanded function arguments are evaluated is unspecified, so g(f(args)...) may call f on the last element first. Folds over the comma operator, and braced initializer lists like int dummy[] = {(f(args), 0)...};, do guarantee left to right. If order matters (printing, side effects), use ((f(args)), ...). For || and && folds, short-circuiting and left-to-right order also hold.

Before C++26 you cannot write args[i]; you unpack the pack into a container or tuple, or recurse. Simple options: std::get<I>(std::forward_as_tuple(args...)) when I is a compile-time constant, or a runtime index with int i = 0; ((i++ == idx ? out = args : 0), ...); to fold over the pack. With 5 arguments and idx 2, the fold touches each once and stores the third. C++26 adds args...[I] directly.

code.title: Perfect forwarding keeps value category

followUps:
template<class T>
T&& fwd(std::remove_reference_t<T>& t) noexcept {
    return static_cast<T&&>(t);
}

It is just a conditional cast. For an lvalue call, T = X&, so T&& collapses to X& and the argument stays an lvalue; for an rvalue call, T = X, so it casts to X&&. The remove_reference_t blocks deduction so you must write fwd<T>(x) explicitly.

Because {1, 2} has no type, so a template parameter pack Args&&... cannot deduce what it is. emplace_back is a forwarding template, and deduction from a braced list fails. Fixes: name the type, v.emplace_back(Point{1, 2}), or use push_back({1, 2}) which takes a known value_type parameter, or emplace_back(1, 2) to pass the constructor arguments separately.

Constrain it so it does not match when the argument is the class itself. Typical C++20 form: template<class T> requires (!std::same_as<std::remove_cvref_t<T>, Wrapper>) Wrapper(T&& v);. Without this, copying a non-const Wrapper w2(w1); prefers the forwarding constructor (exact match Wrapper&) over the copy constructor taking const Wrapper&. Before C++20 the same check is written with std::enable_if_t.

code.title: Type traits built by specialization

followUps: Because the standard library's own code relies on those traits having exactly the defined meaning, and the standard forbids adding specializations of most of them, so doing it is undefined behavior. If you made std::is_integral<MyBigInt> true, library code could treat your class as a built-in and use bit tricks or conversions that do not exist for it. The tiny exceptions are the ones the standard names, such as std::hash or std::common_type for your own types. For your own checks, write your own trait.

std::declval<T>() gives you an expression of type T&& without constructing anything, so you can ask what an operation would return even if T has no default constructor. It is declared but never defined because it is only valid inside unevaluated contexts such as decltype, sizeof and requires-expressions; calling it for real is a compile error. Example: decltype(std::declval<A>() + std::declval<B>()) is the type of a + b.

code.title: SFINAE and enable_if

followUps: The idiom uses std::void_t, an alias that is always void if its arguments are valid types and a substitution failure if not. A partial specialization template<class T> struct has_size<T, std::void_t<decltype(std::declval<T>().size())>> : std::true_type {}; is only chosen if .size() is valid; otherwise the primary template (with default parameter void, deriving false_type) is used. So has_size<std::vector<int>>::value is true and has_size<int>::value is false, with no hard error.

Because SFINAE is hard to read and write: the requirement is hidden in odd places like default template arguments, errors are pages long, and you cannot order two constraints. Concepts give a name to the requirement (std::integral), put it in the signature, give short diagnostics such as "constraint not satisfied: T is not integral", and rank overloads by subsumption. With enable_if, two overloads with overlapping conditions are simply ambiguous; with concepts the more constrained one wins.

code.title: if constexpr vs concepts vs enable_if

followUps: Yes you can write it, but outside a template the discarded branch is still fully checked, so it must be valid code. Only in a template, and only when the condition depends on a template parameter, does the false branch get thrown away without instantiation. Example: in a non-template if constexpr (false) { undefinedName(); } still fails to compile, whereas in template<class T> void f(T x) { if constexpr (!is_integral_v<T>) x.foo(); } for T = int the call x.foo() is discarded and never compiled, but for T = std::string it is checked and never compiled.

End the chain with a branch that is only valid if nothing matched, using a condition that depends on the type, since static_assert(false) alone fails early in older compilers. Pattern: else static_assert(always_false_v<T>, "unsupported type"); where template<class> inline constexpr bool always_false_v = false;. If T is int and an earlier branch handles it, the assert is discarded; for an unhandled type it fires with your message. C++23 makes plain static_assert(false) in templates legal.

code.title: Four concept syntaxes and requires-expression

followUps: The first requires starts a requires clause (a constraint on the template) and the second starts a requires-expression (a list of operations to check). So template<class T> requires requires(T a, T b) { a + b; } T add(T a, T b); means: this function exists only if a + b is valid for T. It is legal but a bit ugly; usually you give the expression a name with concept Addable = requires(T a, T b) { a + b; }; and write requires Addable<T> instead.

Not by the compiler; a concept only checks that code compiles and that return types fit, never that the operation behaves correctly. A type with operator< that is not a strict weak order still satisfies std::totally_ordered. The meaning (axioms such as irreflexivity and transitivity) is documented in the concept's description and is your responsibility. Example: a float class where NaN < x is always false passes the concept but can make std::sort misbehave.

code.title: Constraint subsumption

followUps: Because deciding whether two arbitrary expressions mean the same thing is not possible in general, so the compiler only compares the exact source form after expanding named concepts. std::is_integral_v<T> written in two places are two different atoms, even though they obviously agree. Using a named concept makes them share one atom, so subsumption works. This is why you should write constraints as concepts you reuse rather than copy raw expressions.

Give one of the two a constraint that includes the other, or add a third, more specific overload. For example, if both Hashable and Printable are satisfied, define concept Both = Hashable<T> && Printable<T>; and an overload constrained with it, because Both subsumes each of them. Alternatively dispatch with if constexpr inside a single function, or call a differently named function explicitly.

code.title: Dependent names: typename, template, this->

followUps: Here is the bug and the fix. In template<class T> struct D : Base<T> { void f() { count = 1; } }; the compiler errors with "count was not declared", because Base<T> depends on T and could be specialized with no count, so unqualified lookup skips it. Fixes: write this->count = 1;, or Base<T>::count = 1;, or add using Base<T>::count; in the class. Worse, a global count would be silently picked instead, which is the nasty version of the bug.

MSVC's old permissive mode did not really do two-phase lookup: it parsed templates loosely and looked up many names only at instantiation. So code with a missing typename or an unqualified dependent-base member would compile on MSVC but fail on GCC or Clang. The /permissive- switch (default for new projects since VS 2019 with /std:c++20) turns on conforming behavior. If porting code, expect to add typename, this-> and template keywords in many places.

code.title: Thin templates and type erasure

followUps: Prefer std::function when the callback is stored, crosses a library boundary, or comes in many different types, and prefer a template parameter when it is called in a hot loop. A template parameter gives a distinct type per lambda, lets the compiler inline the call (zero overhead), but generates one copy of the function per callback type. std::function costs an indirect call, possibly a heap allocation for large captures, but gives one compiled function and a uniform type that you can store in a vector. Rough guide: sorting 10 million items, use a template; a button click handler list, use std::function.

Identical code folding can make two different functions share one address, so pointers to them compare equal, which breaks the rule that distinct functions have distinct addresses. If you use function pointers as map keys or identity tokens (for example registering &handlerA and &handlerB), --icf=all may merge them. The safer --icf=safe only folds functions whose addresses are never taken. Use safe mode if your code compares function addresses.
